title: What You Are Actually Measuring When You Benchmark Speculative Decoding Under FP8: A measurement case study on vLLM 0.29.0 and NVIDIA L4
description:
An independent measurement study of speculative decoding and FP8 quantization on vLLM 0.29.0 / NVIDIA L4 (SM89), released with the harness, the raw records, and the full history of its own corrections.

We set out to measure how FP8 quantization interacts with speculative decoding and could not, four times, until the measurement apparatus itself was fixed. Four confounds are identified and quantified:

  1. Attention-backend selection is conditioned on KV-cache dtype. At BF16 KV vLLM selects FlashAttention-2; at fp8_e4m3 it selects FlashInfer, so a precision A/B under default settings is also a kernel A/B. Target and draft models select independently, so pinning one does not pin the other.
  2. Speculative throughput falls into one of two regimes, and the platform decides which. The ratio of CUDA-graph to --enforce-eager throughput, measured in the same container, splits into 0.487–0.768 or 1.003–1.039 with nothing between, and the same partition separates boot-to-boot dispersion (3.73–10.38% against 0.86–1.95%); pooled over 116 boots the two groups do not overlap. Every deficit session shares one configuration — vLLM 0.29.0, DFlash, the L4, NVIDIA driver 580.95.05, on the Modal serverless platform — and every session differing from it in one factor is at parity. Earlier releases read the split first as an engine-release regression and then as a session-scoped random regime; both readings had compared sessions across two host drivers without knowing it. An intervention settles what the records cannot: the same driver, installed by hand on a rented GCP L4 with torch, vLLM, the CUDA image, the model runner and async scheduling all matched, gives parity (ratio 1.001, 95% CI [0.989, 1.013]), and so does the same container pinned to one CPU (1.028). The deficit does not reproduce off the platform it was measured on.
  3. Acceptance length has a boot-to-boot coefficient of variation below 0.88% in every session we have run — nine sessions, three engine releases, both throughput regimes, mean tau within 2.2% throughout — which we could not find reported. That contrast is the point: on the same boots, what the drafter gets accepted is reproducible and how fast it is produced is not. The contrast is itself regime-dependent, which sharpens it: in deficit sessions throughput dispersion exceeds acceptance dispersion by 12–22x, while in parity sessions both are below 2%.
  4. "Inter-token latency" is inter-chunk latency when computed from stream-arrival timestamps. A speculative step emits every accepted token in one chunk, so at concurrency 64 a p95-ITL objective scores the highest-throughput configuration at zero compliant goodput, at every threshold from 20 to 75 ms. This one does not add error, it inverts the decision.

The first three add error; the fourth reverses the ranking.

On the mechanism. Five candidates are eliminated by direct measurement rather than left unexamined: CUDA-graph mode and attention-backend selection (engine logs), power throttling (the driver's own throttle reasons, across arms and across regimes), CPU starvation (a container pinned to one CPU stays at parity), and the host driver on its own (an intervention on rented hardware). The engine itself sees none of it: across every graph-arm log, no message separates the deficit configuration from its neighbours. The platform's sandbox is what remains. Modal documents gVisor for its sandboxes, and gVisor's GPU proxy must support each host driver version exactly, so on Modal a driver change cannot happen without a sandbox change. We name it as the leading candidate by elimination, not as the cause: current gVisor does not list 580.95.05 among its supported drivers, so Modal's sandbox could not be reproduced faithfully. The methodological point stands without that answer: a GPU benchmark on a serverless platform includes a layer the user can neither see nor pin, and that layer changed during this study without notice and moved the CUDA-graph path's throughput by up to a factor of two.

Contents of this archive: the LaTeX source and PDF of the paper; 45 numbered findings, of which 8 are formal retractions and several more withdraw a reading of their own predecessor, each carrying a mandatory "what this does NOT establish" section; the raw append-only measurement records; the analysis scripts that derive every table in the paper from those records; and the audit scripts that verify every numeric claim traces to a stored record and that no finding rests on terminal output.

Reproducibility: every result is re-derivable by a third party on rented hardware. Requires a CUDA GPU of compute capability 8.6 or above and roughly 22 GiB of VRAM. The harness never imports the engine; it launches vLLM as a separate server process and speaks only HTTP. Engine version, host driver, physical GPU identity, platform, visible CPUs, and achieved clocks, power draw and utilisation during the measurement window are recorded per measurement. A harness for running the same measurement on a plain GCP VM, with a hand-installed driver, is included (cloud/gcp/). Two disclosed provenance defects (F009, F014) rest on probe output predating per-measurement recording; neither is cited in the paper and both are disclosed in its threats section.

Licensing: the harness and analysis code are MIT (see LICENSE). The measurements, findings and the paper are CC BY 4.0 (see LICENSE-DATA). The split is deliberate: the harness should be reusable with minimal friction, and the scientific record should carry attribution.

This is a preprint. It has not been peer reviewed.
notes: Measurements were taken on rented NVIDIA L4 and A10 instances, on the Modal serverless platform and on Google Cloud VMs. Physical GPU identity (gpu_uuid) has been recorded per measurement since 2026-09-29, achieved SM clock, power draw and driver throttle reasons across the measurement window since 2026-10-04, and GPU utilisation since 2026-10-31; measurements taken before those dates lack the corresponding fields, and the paper states which of its claims are replicated and which are single-session draws. Every session reported here ran on a distinct physical card, so no regime can be attributed to a specific card. Zenodo's GitHub integration adds its own isSupplementTo relation to the release, so this file deliberately declares none.
